newsitem.title: INDIA: Asia's natural gas demand seen surging.
newsitem.headline: Asia's natural gas demand seen surging.

text.p: Asia's demand for natural gas is expected to increase sharply in coming years, requiring large amounts of investment in gas infrastructure, a senior official of the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Tuesday.
"Of all forms of energy in Asia, natural gas has the strongest growth prospects," IEA executive director Robert Priddle said in a speech prepared for delivery in the Indian capital.

IEA estimates that growing demand for gas and limited availability within Asia could lead it to import up to 40 percent of internationally traded gas supplies from outside the region by 2010, he said.
Asia's demand for liquified natural gas was expected to more than double between 1994 and 2010, he said, citing an IEA study.
"A huge amount of investment in gas infrastructure will be required -- some $20 billion for the ASEAN countries alone," he said referring to the Association of South East Asian Nations.
Priddle said oil, although still very important, was no longer the world's dominant fuel.
He said its share in the world's total primary energy supply had dropped to around 40 percent in 1993 from 50 percent in the early 1970s.

Priddle said commercial energy was progressively replacing non-commercial energy in developing countries, while in industrialised countries more and more energy was being supplied by network industries such as electricity and gas.

Priddle was in India to participate in the International Energy Conference in Goa, where ministers and senior officials from both energy producing and consuming countries will discuss issues of common interest.
The conference, the fifth in a series, was scheduled to run from December 6 to 8.
He said in earlier years energy security was thought of primarily in terms of reducing oil dependence and preparing for an oil supply emergency.
"Today, energy security is seen as relating to energy markets in general, rather than just oil, and being closely linked to environmental sensitivity," Priddle said.
He said energy policy makers, recognising the importance of uncertainity in energy markets, had proposed new approaches.
"A flexible energy sector is now seen as the best guardian against challenges and risks which are unforeseen -- or indeed, unforseeable," Priddle said.

"Despite the present resilience of non-OPEC offshore oil production, in the period 2000-2010 rising global oil consumption and increasing dependence on supplies from the Middle East could again bring energy security concerns to the fore," he added.
Priddle said the most important measure that consumers could take was to build and maintain emergency stocks. But this was expensive and demanded considerable political will, he added.
